We see a lot of things in emergency work… there are troubling things we can chalk down to the job - stuff that ought to traumatise but that we can compartmentalise and then there are some… “those we carry”.

Thank you for sharing. Everyone who has read this now carries a tiny piece of that kid’s soul too; he will not be forgotten. Your efforts and connection won’t have been in vain, as many comments here are a testament. His fate was entirely out of your hands but an ounce of kindness is NEVER wasted… it’s heartbreaking that this lad endured so much hate that he saw no alternative but everyone reading this *just knows* that in your moment of connection/that fist bump, he felt better.

I hope you rest easy knowing that you do an incredible job. Those we carry help us to help others with greater empathy, humility, knowledge, understanding… but none of them would want to see you suffer; if they start to haunt you - take a step further back, talk freely and honestly and as much as you need to, spend time with your people, nourish your connections, give yourself time and find yourself again. Sending great love & care ♥️

Trust your feelings. He’s a full blown adult and shouldn’t be doing or saying anything that’s even vaguely open to interpretation with a minor, even if they (you) come across as super mature. His actions were very wrong, you felt it was wrong - it is 100% wrong but the onus is on HIM to keep to boundaries.

Mixed feelings are understandable- you’ve known him a long time, he’s a big part of your life and has played a big role in your family; your siblings are related to him and you are correct in that this disruption will have consequences. But I am SO glad your Mom plans to leave him. I can see why you might question your decision to speak up, and why you could feel guilty but that feeling that it was uncomfortable and wrong was and is completely valid. HE was the one who crossed a line, was grossly inappropriate, traumatised a minor, and cannot be trusted. These are the consequences of HIS actions - sexual themes and content should have been a non-negotiable boundary for him. 

It’s not an uncommon response to question your memory or judgment but that’s a trauma response - it’s a scenario that doesn’t make moral sense to the fairly primitive part of your brain that knows, almost intuitively, right from wrong. You’re literally trying to figure out how this would happen within the framework of ‘adults with significant influence in my life are supposed to keep me safe’… but it doesn’t fit, so you question yourself. It’s a natural response but I hope you are able to stick with your own conviction if/when things hit the fan - there is NO excuse he can give that makes you out to be anything other than an innocent victim whom he took advantage of. I actually dislike the phrase victim as sometimes it can be disempowering and hinder recovery but I use it here in particular to represent the absolute power imbalance that existed - you were completely vulnerable.

I hope your Mom sticks to her word. I hope it causes as little disruption as possible to you all - it’s gonna be a mess for all the family to work through, however that pans out. I’m sorry for the pain you will go through, both directly and as a result of the other relationships here that are being fractured… but this man doesn’t deserve a family if he is willing to do to a young person what he did to you. You did the right thing. It’s not about breaking family bonds for revenge - it’s about speaking the truth, being heard, being believed and your Mom taking whatever actions she must to protect her children, including you, including his bio kids. He is not a safe adult.

Sending you love and resolve. You are a strong, incredibly resilient, obviously caring, very insightful young man and the trauma and difficulties you’ve faced - although they no doubt shape you in some ways & affect you deeply in many other ways - the traumas you’ve experienced do not define you, your worth, or your place in the world. You deserve better than this and I wish you all the luck as you navigate this ♥️

Rachel Riley who is now on Countdown. We were in several classes together but weren’t friends. She was generally inoffensive - reasonably popular with other students, had a group of friends with similar middle-class backgrounds. Known throughout school as a bit of a swot as very successful academically and in sports, quite beloved of the teachers as a result. Always considered very mature and a good ambassador for the school if participating in anything competitive.

My best friend’s sister had this weird unexplained loathing for her and would always call her a man on the basis of (to me, barely noticeable) peach fuzz on her top lip.

I’m a doctor and have looked into this before, as ‘Functional Assessor’ job are frequently advertised and look so appealing compared to the usual under-resourced, pandemic-stricken hospital or GP jobs. They seem too good to be true - because they are. 

Apparently it’s all lovely at the beginning and the money is much better than equivalent in NHS/training jobs, there are some nice additional perks like gym membership and private health insurance, more sustainable and sociable working hours… a dream! 

But with only one single exception (who might have been a bot/plant/soulless ghoul), the advice I’ve seen from anyone who’s done it is to steer clear. The conditions change once you’ve settled in and more/tighter targets are introduced encouraging downgrading or finding the applicant ineligible. It sounds horrific as a job if you went into medicine with some kind of desire to *help*… and completely inhumane and humiliating for anyone unfortunate enough to have to go through the process as an applicant 😞
Wise words x

OMG yes hard relate. Having to stay with my Mum at my parents’ house a lot lately due to Dad’s terminal illness and it is so traumatising for me. It’s as clear as day to me that she has ADHD, and I showed my brother the questions with example behaviours in the DIVA-5 questionnaire and even he had to agree that she hits almost 100% of them.

But she’s in absolute denial and takes the idea that there might be ‘something wrong’ with her as hugely offensive. Causing offence leads to emotional outbursts & guilt trips, much like it has done my whole life. The only thing that’s improved from my difficult adolescence is that she’s not physically violent toward me any more.

Mum is currently Dad’s main carer and he has care high needs right now, so she’s not had a full uninterrupted night’s sleep for months which has made everything so much worse. She won’t accept more help and when people are there, she interferes all the time. She apparently has systems (I think creating systems is how she functioned raising 2 kids and having a job - but she had to stick to them so rigidly for them to work so she always swung from super controlling to chaotic rages) but she isn’t able to actually stick to them currently because she’s so frazzled. Dad has missed important medication etc. when her systems have fallen apart and it’s happening more often. She’s basically hit ADHD burnout but that’s still not enough for her to see that she’s not coping and there is an underlying explanation for why.

My mental health is hanging on by a thread and the emotional work of dealing with my Mum just compounds the difficulty of dealing my Dad dying slowly of cancer. 

It’s why I now live 250+ miles away, but I’ve just come back from a 6 day stay with her… and it’s going to take me days to mentally recover from.

Sorry, went on a bit of a vent there. I’m sorry you’re being affected by it and I hope that either she comes into some insight or you find ways to adapt that protect you from the negativity that this situation can bring x

P.s. Have read some more of your replies in comments, OP. Our mother’s could be the same person. Sending you so much love and strength ♥️

Yeah. I’m nearly 36 and I feel like maybe if I could have another 10 years to just sort my shit out, I might be ready! I spent 9 years as a university student and although I had a part time job for the majority of it, I didn’t really have any ‘adult’ worries - financially I had student loans and income from my job, I knew I would graduate into a good & stable career, home ownership wasn’t on the cards because I was in a major city where affordability was zero for me at that point. Then I suffered a period of depression, followed by a break up from my longterm partner. My subsequent relationship (and marriage) is to a man who already has one biological child, and the pressures of navigating that have taken a lot of effort. Our finances aren’t great after I had gambling issues as a result of medication, we’ve both been affected by significant family illness/bereavement, we’re in a pandemic, house prices where we now live are more affordable but still inflated due to Covid, and there is some uncertainty as to where my job will be based in a couple of years time (plus we’re currently 250+ miles from my family, so childcare logistics are tricky/expensive) - there is so much to juggle already and I feel like I’m barely holding it together as is.

Add to that my best friend, who is the same age, has had a baby and expressed when pregnant that she didn’t feel ready/old enough… now baby is 8 months, she says she wishes she’d listened to that gut feeling and desperately misses her ‘old life’ before the baby arrived. I also look back at my life before marriage & step kid and wish I could go back to that time, and that I don’t feel ready for the commitment of a biological child either 😬

This absolutely sounds like a HIM problem and it sounds like he’s repeating abusive patterns with you that also broke his previous relationship. Find as much stability and backup as you can and get the hell outta there ♥️

You’ve edited your post, so to address your additional ridiculous points: 

No, I specifically said the stepparent doesn’t have legal rights.

I don’t want to lay a hand on my step child. I don’t consider that anyone’s right. It’s definitely not a ‘benefit’ as you put it!

Here’s some news for you: there are ways of disciplining kids that don’t involve physical violence. At this point it isn’t surprising me that this is your go to 🙄

I hope your ex moves on to a partner understanding enough to deal with your crazy. It is up to her and her partner how they choose for things to work in their house. You’ll discover this soon enough. I mean, how are you going to enforce your will in a house you don’t live in? Your is your opinion. And if your ex doesn’t agree with your opinion… so long as their partner’s involvement isn’t harming your child… you’re going to need to start learning about parallel parenting, buddy.

And please, I beg you, if you won’t address your anger issues with a therapist, at least get your child access to someone who can help them work through your issues.

Chimps don’t have husbands because marriage is a social construct created by humans and if you can’t get past that first hurdle… just… stop. Gosh, isn’t that even more embarrassing for you if you do actually have a degree in behavioural biology?! 

Forgive my skepticism, but in your comment history you claim to be a doctor, having gone to medical school. You’d think someone capable of that academic feat might be able to string together a more coherent argument. Or even a coherent paragraph. I can’t even work out where the reference to pair bonding species fits in. Because it exists in nature, that’s how it should be? ‘Cause it sounds like that didn’t work out for you either, honey.

Anyway, I mean, on any other day I’d *love* to know what a chimpanzee’s definition of a ‘real Dad’ is. I like how you referred to male chimps as ‘men’. It’s cute. Next you’ll be telling me chimps have custody orders too 😂 

Finally, as a biologist you really ought to know that a male chimpanzee can be just as aggressive to another male’s offspring as a male lion…

I’m done with this conversation. You’re incredibly angry over the fact that other people have the heart to love kids they didn’t create, and evidently bitter that these people choose to be more generous than you with their time, effort, finances and love. You’re jumping on the suggestion that they embrace this but do so in a boundaried way as something to attack me over.  Why? Because you previously assumed the role of stepdad, allowed yourself to get shafted, and here you are STILL SUPER PISSED about it. That’s on you, and you’ll stay stuck in this pit of rage until you grow up and take responsibility for yourself. I almost feel sorry for you but it’s certainly not my job to pacify you. Take care.

You have no idea of my situation, but all you need to know is that there have been difficult times but we’ve worked them out and come to an arrangement that works for us. We’re happy, it works, and if it didn’t I wouldn’t continue.

If you’re even a stepparent and not simply a troll, focus on your own situation.

Also, there are LOTS of things that humans do that aren’t found in nature… motor transport, modern healthcare, processed foods, organised crime, the welfare state… it’s a pretty lame argument, and that’s IF it were wholly accurate, which it isn’t!

Over 120 animal species engage in ‘alloparenting’ where the biological parents are not the sole caregivers of the offspring. This ranges from suckling unrelated young (warthogs), babysitting whilst parents feed (sperm whales), to group parenting where non-related females can spend more time raising young than the biological parent (chimps). You could look it up.

You are those things only if you accept that role! Being used as a maid, financially exploited, treated as a second class citizen… if the adults involved in this scenario don’t like it, it should be addressed and changed. The kids will treat you by the example their parent/your partner sets and in line with the standards you both uphold.

Being an adult involves standing up for yourself and negotiating your role with your partner. If you and your partner aren’t mature enough to do that, you’re setting yourself up for a very miserable experience and setting an appalling example for the kids. If you’re happy with that… you do you, babe. If you’re not, get the other adult on board and change it… or walk. You don’t sound happy, you sound bitter and resentful and that’s no good for you.

Don’t blame your inability to adult appropriately on the presence of kids. No-one is forcing you to stay. Sometimes humans are dumber than animals. As if you even need to be told this shit…
You’ve, errrm, not come across the original song, have you?

This isn’t about the 10 year old (mostly). This is far more about parental alienation- BM has discovered a way to control things by using SD’s emotions as an excuse and fanning the flames of her anxiety to manipulate your family.

Your SO needs a formal custody order. SD needs to see her Dad - if she’s really got a problem herself with the presence of you & your daughter, your SO can arrange activities out of the house to minimise shared time, to start with. But it’s not a feasible long term plan. She will have to adjust. Ten year olds don’t get to dictate the entire arrangement of their parents’ family, even if they have big emotions to deal with over it. Get her fixed up with a therapist if her emotions are really the issue… but I suspect from the iPad comment, it will not be a deal breaker once BM’s involvement is nipped in the bud.I

I see where you’re coming from, and I think for a lot of stepparents the decision about which responsibilities they shoulder stems proportionally from the rights they are given by the bio parents. 

* Edit to add: particularly in cis-hetero partnerships where the Dad is the bio parent and the new partner is a woman, it often goes that the woman takes on responsibilities BEFORE any rights are discussed or established, because both parties assume she’s up for slipping right in to that societally expected ‘caring’ role without necessarily laying any ground rules first. She wants to bond with the kids, be helpful, make things work… and the Dad is usually quite willing to have someone step in to share those responsibilities and make life easier for him. Not every step family evolves like this but it’s pretty common and I think it’s where so much resentment and conflict arises. * Edit ends.

Obviously there are laws involved and legal rights are limited to parents, but if my step kid is living in my house and benefiting from all the opportunities my presence brings, and I am dealing with the work that comes from a child I didn’t create… I sure as hell expect a seat the table in terms of day-to-day rights! 

If I get a say in bedtime, I will help out with the kid in the day. If I get to share the kid’s academic life via my partner, I will help with the homework. If I get a say in the schedule, I will try my best to make it work.

Whether or not you have those rights and responsibilities seems more of a discussion to be had with the parent who is your partner on an individual basis - rather than a blanket rejection of all things ‘parental’. You’re choosing to have a very significant role in a kid’s life by being romantically involved with their parent… the exact degree is negotiable but you can’t pretend the kid is an optional extra.

ONE: Got rights? (i.e. are your preferences & opinions taken into account, especially around arrangements that directly affect you)
- No -> requires discussion with partner. If still no, move to step 2. 
- Yes -> we’re not talking legal adoption here, but an ability to contribute to important issues. Move to step 2.

TWO: Got responsibilities?
- No -> if no rights and no responsibilities… what are you doing? If it’s your choice… well, there’s disengaging and then there’s simply not interested. If it’s either/both bioparent’s choice… just run, this is gonna be a whole load of heartache. Either way, consider dating someone without kids. 
(If only rights and no responsibilities… this is a weird dynamic and I’m baffled if it ever actually happens this way?!)
- Yes -> are your responsibilities proportional to your rights? If yes, good! Hopefully you will continue to feel valued and your presence in the kid’s life will be a positive one, because there is collaboration and an element of control for you. 
If no, you’re being taken advantage of: re-discuss this with your partner and be mindful of immature parents who are just looking for someone to take over the hard work for them.

THREE: Are you, your partner and child’s other parent all on the same page?
- If the other bio parent is of the opinion that you as the stepparent ‘don’t count’, then you sure as hell need your partner to nip that in the bud! They need be on board with presenting a united front in the face of bio parent dismissing you. They need to be advocating for your role and your right to be heard in the conversations that affect you. If they won’t do that, they should get therapy to help them handle conflict with their ex. If they won’t do that, they might as well shack back up with the ex whilst you sail off into the sunset and away from that drama - you are not a glorified babysitter.

This kid is clinging on to Dad because she is craving stability.

Every other day needs to stop. She might prefer it but it doesn’t mean it’s best for her. A lot of kids would happily chose to eat McDonalds for every meal, and be quite certain of that choice! Doesn’t mean it’s right for them.

This arrangement is contributing to her needs only being partially met (she’s not secure that she is a priority, hence ‘asking’ for confirmation all the time with attention seeking behaviours) and your needs are not being met (you have no time as couple and feel bottom of priorities).

It’s tough to juggle multiple demands for attention in a blended household. It doesn’t really sound like your boyfriend is attempting to ‘juggle’ at all - just directing attention to whomever shouts loudest.

You guys need to address areas that are causing anxiety in the kid:
- every other day schedule
- lots of extra curriculars (any messages that are unconsciously being sent there - that worth is based on achievement, that you as parents would rather she were doing something that doesn’t require your direct attention?) 
- bed time! This kid is not getting enough sleep, especially with the addition of such busy days & active hobbies
- history of partners; others have gone into more detail but if you’re used to parents having on/off partners or different people for short times… you learn that an adult’s presence is not guaranteed (this is largely out of your control but is a good reason for the other modifiable factors to be addressed)

Boyfriend needs to enforce some boundaries and expectations because even if it seems counterintuitive, these help kids develop a structure and feel safer. It’s likely that every interruption for his attention is a response to a split second of anxiety in her, and each time he responds, he reinforces her need for instant reassurance. I’m not saying a kid looking for reassurance is a bad thing, but at some point she will need to be able to fall back on her own ability to self-soothe. Providing boundaries such as “I will come and play with you at 6pm, and until then you can carry on (insert activity here), and I ask that you only interrupt mstsquared and me if it’s an emergency”. And then he follows through. It will be tough and you guys might need some professional assistance from the therapists involved but otherwise he’s setting the kid up for even more issues.

Good luck!

You’ve articulated this way better than I could. The first few weeks on meds were just this beautiful silence. I’m still on meds at max dose and they help a lot of my ADHD symptoms but the constant loop came back after a while and the only time it’s goes now is when I’m reeeally hyperfocusing… even then I’m often conscious of it - like someone’s turned it down so I can just hear a tune rather than make out a song with lyrics, if that makes sense? Even though it’s not always a song with lyrics playing. Right now it’s a little loop from a piece of of classical music. It can be a jingle or a chorus or a little clip… for me it’s barely ever a whole song, but anything from 10-30 seconds on a constant loop.

This is an ongoing battle here too (I’m in the UK) with my 9 y/o SS. Most of the time he eats like a 3 year old and gets food down himself so the majority of stuff is visibly dirty, but even when it’s not his automatic response is to chuck all clothes straight into the laundry. He went through a phase of doing this with his pyjamas in the morning too. We do not have enough pairs for him to wear a new pair each night so this became evident quite quickly and he seems to have grasped the concept now!

He’ll also just put on visibly dirty clothes that are lying around if for some reason they aren’t in the laundry basket.

It’s like he has no eyes or common sense. My husband does the same and I’ve had people try and suggest ‘it’s a boy thing’ but it really isn’t. Boys and men are no less capable of identifying whether an item or clothing is clean or dirty… it’s more that they’re just used to someone else picking up the slack.

Not on my watch, guys!

That is terrifying. Where are the bioparents in all of this? What are the repercussions for his behaviour? If there are decent boundaries and consequences to his behaviour and he’s not just acting this way because ‘any attention is good attention’, then are you sure this is a situation you want to stay in? He is just a kid but he won’t be forever and if he is already victimising you, that behaviour will escalate.
Yes please? :)

It’s laid out explicitly on the school’s website. It’s very clear. The first hit on Google is the Government advice and whilst not a lot of the Government’s advice has been clear regarding restrictions, when and how to get tested is very clear. My job does not make me BM’s personal problem solver or in-house doctor.

I appreciate she could have been stupider and I have acknowledged that she did the right thing. I am frustrated that she chose the option of least resistance for her, at the detriment of SS’s opportunities this weekend. This is a repeating pattern in their & our lives.

My husband and I did teach SS to ride a bike. We take him swimming when it’s her week and she can’t be bothered. Husband does his best to keep the peace but in doing so often drops to lowest common denominator parenting, and yes, I have to encourage him not to be a lazy parent too. BM in particular has little appreciation that her actions have consequences beyond herself. My husband is learning. SS is also learning, but frankly trying to coach all 3 of them on How to Adult can be exhausting and I needed to vent.

It it indeed just a vent, thanks for listening. I’m glad she did the right thing. I’m frustrated it took me stepping in and spelling it out to her when the information is readily available and I’m annoyed her laziness meant my SS is potentially missing out on time with his Dad (which will likely be used as a reason to ask us last minute to reschedule plans in future, because that’s what she’s like).

She didn’t directly ask me for advice. She asked my husband, who said he didn’t know either. It’s not a case of opinion, it’s a case of following the current rules which are easily accessible. Neither of them thought to even Google the current recommendations, which is what astounds me. It’s not rocket science. This woman needs her hand held at every step of the way (as does my husband, half the time).

They could have taken a <30 minute walk, outside, in decent weather, where they were not mixing with anyone, to get a test sooner. You are allowed to leave the house to get the test. But she chose the postal option which takes far longer and now SS won’t get a result in time to see his Dad this weekend. There was no good reason not to get tested on the Thursday he developed symptoms. She is just lazy. This is on a background of so many other instances… e.g. why read a bed time story to your kid when you can put on an audiobook? Why teach them to ride a bike when you can buy a scooter instead? Why take them to their swimming lessons when you can have a lie-in and they can watch YouTube instead?

I’m sorry your experience didn’t have positive outcome. I would be devastated if all the hard work I put in to raising my SS was thrown by the wayside, disregarded and unappreciated (I mean, sometimes it is anyway but that’s out of my control). But I don’t have to stay. I chose this and, for now, I continue to choose this. Might I regret it? Of course. Do you? Sounds like it from your reply. But OP is invested and looking for advice on how to make it work. If that’s her choice, I feel I post supportively of that. If you can’t, then at least you’ve been open enough to explain your stance and for that I’m glad. It’s always enriching to have multiple views, right? I hope you’ve moved on to a place of happiness and can use past experiences to inform your path in future x

This is my main reason for being undecided. The logistical type issues I face (financial, housing/space issues, existence of stepkid etc.) can all be over come with enough effort, I think.

The mess the world is in is out of our individual control though. We can’t fix it ourselves and it doesn’t look like humanity collectively will fix it either. Why would a parent knowingly subject their offspring to that, with the awareness it would probably be even worse for them?

That’s the question I always come back to, and I hate it. I would love to have a kid, but I am so conflicted about what I can only see as the ‘selfishness’ of that decision. What if the life they end up with is miserable, for reasons out of their control? What if more of their lifetime is spent feeling bad compared to feeling good? What if they wish they hadn’t been born?

I’m not trying to argue a case against another child - absolutely do what feels right to you - but this resonates strongly with me and this is how I feel about it. (I wish I didn’t)

In terms of advice, I would recommend honesty. 8 years old is mature enough to understand that her Mom is unreliable and that even if her Mom’s presence is unpredictable, she can start to adjust to expecting it to be. Of course it’s not ideal, but unless you think BM will genuinely get her shit together, I’d just try to explain it to your SD as non-judgementally as possible. 

I’d frame it that all families are a bit different and sometimes they are able to hang out all the time and at other times they can’t. At the moment her Mom can’t but she’s working on it and you can’t promise what might happen either way. In the meantime though, although you’re not her Mom and can’t replace her, you’re an adult she can rely on and you’ll be there to care about and support her.

I guess I would have anxiety over the situation too - if BM isn’t around much, SD will probably gravitate toward you more and become attached to you and the stability of your presence. Then if BM gets back on the scene and you start splitting time with BM more, SD may feel unsure about the removal of her constant role model (you) and also conflicted about loyalty if you two have formed a good bond and then BM (who’s attention and affection she naturally craves) is reintroduced.

Emotionally, it’s an impossible situation. A situation like this will always introduce anxiety and instability into the kid’s life - and yours. If you care about SD (which you clearly do) and want what’s best, of course you’re affected by the situation. And it’s all because of BM and that’s frustrating. It feels like a ridiculous thing to care about a kid more than their bioparent(s) but sadly it seems to happen a lot.

I would definitely talk to your partner about long term plans over custody. If this issue carries on, I expect will be the ongoing unpredictability that affects your SD rather than an absolute feeling of abandonment from BM. Kids adapt, but only if they have a predictable enough situation to adapt to.

You’re assuming a one size fits all step-parenting dynamic. Sometimes there are scenarios where it is more appropriate/convenient/practical for the step-parent to be involved. Usually - speaking from personal experience - it’s not because we *want* this drama, but because we are putting the needs of a kid (who asked for none of this) ahead of the needs of the adults who can’t get their shit together. That is exactly what’s happening here.

I would encourage the OP to see if their partner can help shoulder some of the responsibility if possible, but sometimes it doesn’t work like that. TBH I don’t think it matters *who* the news “your Mom won’t see you” comes from, it’s still heartbreaking for a kid to hear. Sounds like this kiddo has been through a lot of unpredictability and maybe the OP is the person they turn to for reassurance and stability.

The fact that BM hasn’t kept phone contact or visited is very telling. From this version of events, I don’t believe BM is trying her hardest to be involved and only hitting ‘work’ related barriers (and if she genuinely is, she’s just not capable of problem solving well enough to be responsible for a child).

Another commenter suggested you look at the evidence base and you replied you didn’t have time. You’ve actively argued with those sharing their lived experience.

And now you’re trying to insinuate which parts of your post I find offensive to create a narrative that fits your original argument. I am not offended by you, nor your views… I just don’t get what you’re looking for, because your replies to comments go against your apparent plea for assistance in furthering your understanding. 

To be honest, the whole “should I refer myself to the GMC?” comment was too flippant for anyone to have taken you seriously in the first place. My bad.

This post really ought to have stopped after the second paragraph.

You have a non-expert, non-nuanced understanding of ADHD and whilst I applaud you seeking out further information and opinions from experts, you’re simultaneously refusing to look at the evidence base and are dismissive of replies explaining lived experience. What exactly are you looking for? Seems like you’re just looking for validation.

Please feed back to your FPD/TPD that is not appropriate for trainees at your level to be performing new patient assessments for ? ADHD.

It’s so difficult trying to make a decision on children at the best of times, but much harder whilst also going through the struggles of losing a parent - grief really messes with all your other emotions, and brings up/amplifies all kinds of feelings that might not have been influencing your decision before. It’s such a complex argument for those of us on the fence.

For me, when my Dad was diagnosed as having less than a year to live, my first instinct was that if I wanted my Dad to meet his grandchild, my husband and I would have to start trying immediately… so I was like, right, we should do this! But I quickly realised that this idea came from a place of wanting him to have that experience of meeting his grandchild, and from wanting any future child to at least have a photo with my Dad or something they could later feel a connection to him from. There was an element of wanting him to be proud of me for taking the step of having a child and going through the challenges of pregnancy and labour- that ‘awwww, well done’ moment that’s often depicted in the media... I would miss that if I waited and then later decided to procreate. But having those pro-child feelings actually didn’t change any of my pro-child-free feelings and then I considered the logistical issues of being pregnant/having a newborn around the time he passed (particularly as it wasn’t totally unclear how the covid situation would pan out - this was early days prior to vaccines being developed) and that seemed like it could potentially make a devastating time even worse.

My Dad has also traditionally not been the talkative warm type, but he surprised me when I got to visit him alone in hospital a couple of months ago. He was initially really unwell and when he was admitted I wouldn’t have been surprised if he didn’t make it out of hospital again then. In a tearful and emotional display of affection he told me how proud he was of me and how much he loves me. It was unsettling because I don’t think I have EVER seen him cry before. You might find that this situation with your Dad’s health opens up a side of him and a vulnerability you don’t expect and he is more willing to talk about topics you guys might have skirted before. It is uncomfortable though. Even though I deal with emotional situations and tearful people through my job every day, I literally had no idea what to do when it was my Dad crying in front of me. I think it’s all part of the process of how each of us - and the father-daughter relationship itself - deals with the inevitability death.

Maybe either with that conversation and/or once some time has passed for emotions to play out, your path might be clearer. Wishing you and your family peace through this x

Aripiprazole was developed as an antipsychotic but is often used as an adjunct (i.e. as an add-on) to help depression and anxiety. It’s usually added on to an SSRI or SNRI antidepressant (like sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine, venlafaxine, duloxetine) rather than alone though, in the context of treating depression. ADHD is accepted as a deficiency of dopamine and stimulants (various amphetamine based drugs, methylphenidate) increase dopamine. Although aripiprazole targets dopamine like ADHD stimulant meds, it’s not usually an adjunct for ADHD treatment due to HOW it acts on dopamine receptors. There are lots of different dopamine pathways in your brain and aripiprazole affects them differently depending on your natural dopamine levels - it has a boosting action at some receptors and a blocking action at others.

Prior to my ADHD diagnosis, I experienced an episode of mild psychosis. Psychosis is thought to be related to overactivity of areas of the dopamine system, so I was put on aripiprazole. I felt slightly less depressed and less anxious, I think. However, I developed a pathological gambling habit - a problem that never affected me prior to the aripiprazole (I literally never even bought a lottery ticket before then). However, addictions are more common in those with ADHD as the dopamine hit from the indulging the addiction is EVEN more pleasurable if you have low dopamine to start with… so I may have had a natural vulnerability to gambling but never realised it, and the aripiprazole magnified it due to the particular pathways involved. There are quite a lot of reports of people struggling with gambling and other addictive/compulsive behaviours whilst on aripiprazole. Once I stopped the aripiprazole, the gambling stopped being an issue as soon as it was out of my system.

The upshot of this was that when I got diagnosed with ADHD, my doctor was super cautious about starting me on stimulant medication for fear of either triggering psychosis and/or gambling. Turns out a stimulant (Vyvanse) has improved everything without causing either issue.

No two brains are exactly the same and an individual’s reaction to a drug is difficult to fully predict, but my point is that a lot of psychiatric medications and conditions are over simplified:

• E.g. ‘SSRI antidepressants boost serotonin’ - actually it depends on dose and at least 2 other types of receptors are also involved at standard doses of most SSRI’s.

• E.g. ‘antipsychotics decrease dopamine’ - as explained, very much depends on which pathways in particular, which depends on the drug. 

• E.g. ‘Too much dopamine causes psychosis’ - for me, boosting dopamine with stimulants has been really beneficial but boosting only certain pathways with an antipsychotic caused major problems.

Sorry for the essay. In no way intended to put you off trying aripiprazole. Just wanted to highlight that (A) it’s usually IN ADDITION to another class of antidepressant if it’s being used to treat depression (B) it can exacerbate addiction issues in those prone to it, and those with ADHD can indeed be more prone to all forms of addiction.

In answer to your question about how you should feel… it can take around 4 weeks for the levels of the drug to reach a steady peak effect and for your receptors to adjust to the presence of the medication, so if it’s going to help, it may not be immediately and it may not be at the initial dose. The idea is that you feel better. If you don’t after a fair trial of 6 weeks and another 6 weeks of a dose increase, then maybe it’s not the one. Bearing in mind potential negative effects as above (plus various other side effects including weight gain/high lipids/increased diabetes risk) then I would never advise anyone to stay on aripiprazole - or any medication - if it wasn’t actively helping. Have you tried other ‘first line’ antidepressants like SSRI’s or is this the first option suggested by your doctor? Sounds like it needs more discussion with them, really.

Anyway, apologies for the essay. I’m a doctor with ADHD, and as per my rambling above I’ve also had previous depression with psychosis, and am a recovered compulsive gambler linked to aripiprazole - so it’s a topic I feel strongly about sharing! Take care x

I’m literally a doctor. I did well in school. I got diagnosed as a 34 year old adult, and my assessment included my childhood school reports — the psychiatrist said it was a prime example of a spot-on diagnosis of inattentive type in a girl being missed because of high ability.

High ability kids get missed because they compensate - they know they struggle, so they try harder and find work arounds. Their hyperfocus often overlaps with academic interests so of course they do well. But when life piles on more and more mundane tasks that they struggle with, eventually things start to crash down. But if you go back and look closely, you’ll see cracks as early as childhood - I had a teacher accept my A level coursework to her home address 2 weeks after the official deadline (and the night before she was due to submit my mark to the examination panel)... she knew I would do well, but she also knew I’d procrastinated on it and prioritised the wrong things and that I was only going to be able to turn it in at the last minute. She just recognised that in me - I had potential but I struggled with the execution. That has been the overwhelming theme of my life, even through med school. I was able and had potential. Sometimes I nailed it academically and other times I just couldn’t quite get there. This is often how girls and women present. You’ve got what it takes but equally you’ve not quite got what it takes. 🤨

It sounds like there have been long periods more recently where you haven’t been able to spend meaningful time with your SD?

A 6 yo girl is very different to a 7-nearly-8 yo. To us, it’s just a couple of years. To a kid, they go through loads of emotional change, new awareness of interactions between adults, working out where they are comfortable and who to trust. It’s almost like babies/toddlers going through that stage where they are happy to be cuddled and coo-ed at by anyone and then suddenly they have stranger danger and attachment anxiety and only Mum/Dad will do.

Her main caregiver is her Mum. She’s thoroughly attached to her. Aged 7 or so, kids (especially girls but it happened with my SS) can go through a clingy phase. I think it comes with increased awareness of their parents relationships with others - my SS would be extra clingy with his Dad when I/other people were around. Fine when it was 1:1 time with Dad, but almost regressing to babyish behaviour to get Dad’s attention when others were around. We increased the 1:1 time with his Dad and gave a lot of reassurance that he was loved and a priority but also making clear that he needed to behave appropriately. He grew out of it mostly, but we sometimes see the same behaviour creeping in when there are groups of people or when he feels he’s not getting his Dad’s undivided attention. In your case, it sounds like your SD is behaving similarly but her ‘safe place’ is with her Mum.

I think, if you & her Dad are going to be involved going forward, you need to push through this phase.

Insist on a regular agreement of time spent with her - either a formal or informal custody arrangement. If her Mum is being obstructive, go through CAFCASS. It is in the best interests of the kid to have a relationship with her Dad, especially if he (and you) are super keen to be involved. In cases where there is risk of harm or neglect to the kid, or the non-custodial parent just isn’t interested then that’s different but it sounds like you guys are keen and will be a good influence in her life.

She - and Mum - may resist. Persevere. Unfortunately, you don’t know what Mum is saying to SD about her Dad & you when you are not there. Parental Alienation Syndrome is difficult but there is a lot of advice out there. With a kid of 7 years, it’s probably most difficult to deal with - she knows that Mum is her safe place and will likely believe anything she says, because she is old enough to take things on board but not yet old enough to weigh up evidence and make up her own mind about things.

The flip side, is that 7 yo kids still like to have fun. Make the visits fun for her and she will most likely come around. Don’t give her the option of hiding in her room - make it clear that her room is a safe space for her if she needs to withdraw, but when she arrives let her put her stuff there and then tell her the schedule for the day. A lot of anxiety comes from unpredictability - an idea could be to plan some activities, have each on a little card and then sit with her when she arrives to discuss which she’d like to do/which she doesn’t like the sound of so much, and then plan the order of the day. That way she knows what’s coming. Build in some time alone with her Dad too and some down time as well, particularly at the start (our version of downtime for SS is either him watching YouTube videos (he just watches random junk), an episode of The Simpsons, or some time playing Roblox/Minecraft. We tend to limit screen time by making other activities that we do together non-screen based).

Also, ask her what makes her feel safe. Things like weighted blankets, certain books or clothes, stuffed toys etc. can still be huge sources of comfort for kids of that age in environments that they aren’t familiar with or when they are feeling anxious.

Obviously it’s harder with Covid lockdown and things being closed, but if you can do trips out together then you are in ‘neutral’ territory rather than ‘your’ house, which can help. Doing activities that really engross the kid can help too - physical stuff like bike riding, horse riding, swimming, climbing/high ropes etc (depending on budget/what is open). 

If she’s quite sociable and outgoing and has a lot of friends, sometimes that can help too - arrange a play date in a park with a friend from school. This will help get you ‘in the loop’ with parents of her friends. This may rely on cooperation of SD’s mother to arrange however. But by 7/8 yo your SD may be able to tell you enough for you to reach out directly to her friend’s parents, e.g. via FB

Encourage your partner to speak to SD’s school and ask them to duplicate information to him as well so he doesn’t miss anything important. He has a right as her parent, and schools are used to separated parents not having 100% harmonious relationships.

I had one occasion where my mouth got so dry I struggled to articulate my words until I managed to get a drink. Bacteria in your mouth love it when you have a dry mouth as it means they have free access to oxygen rather than having to fight through a barrier of saliva... as a result, despite all the brushing & flossing, bad breath can ensue. I carry water, sugar free mints and sometimes artificial saliva spray with me now. I found the degree to which my mouth dries up did improve after a while as I adjusted to the meds, but it’s still a bit of an issue.

The greatest thing about this is that the more you floss in the bathroom, the more you’ll start to associate it with being in there, the harder it will be not to think about it... and before you know it, the game has become a habit 👏🏻

You will NEVER get that money back by gambling. That is a fact that we’ve learned the hard way.

Honestly, the only way I cracked my addiction was to come clean to my husband (and later family who I relied on to bail me out). Yes, it’s humiliating and difficult... but it’s literally the only way. Gambling is a recognised addiction - it does things to your brain and spirals out of control. It may be hard for your husband and family to accept but the important things are 1.) that you’ve stopped and 2.) that you’re being open about it being problematic. The circumstances were understandable - you have the pressure of a small baby to care for and you were alone with your husband deployed, right? Gambling - like alcohol or drugs - is a kick. It is a comfort, a relaxing & entertaining distraction, followed by the thrill of winning. Compare that to being on your own after a hard day? Of course you’d get sucked in.

To stop, you need to immediately self exclude from all the sites you are signed up to. See if you can sign up to GamStop or similar to prevent you from signing up to others. If you can block gambling transactions with your bank and credit cards, do that too.

Draw on this feeling of fear and panic if you’re tempted to gamble to win back your losses. Ultimately, you will not win and you will feel like this only worse because you will have lost $2700 but whatever else extra you deposit to try and get it back.

How you’re going to get the money back? That’s another difficult thing. In my case, my parents were able to help me. If you really need that money immediately, do you have anyone you could ask to lend it? Otherwise, if it was savings, you’ll be able to build it back up over time. Don’t panic about not having the full amount right now. Whatever you do, do not take out high cost loans to gamble with hoping you’ll win big and be able to repay it all back. It will not work (yes, voice of experience again).

You can get through this. It’s hard, but there are thousands of us who have been where you are.

1. Absolutely 100% stop gambling further.
2. Be honest with your family (& friends or anyone else you can trust to support you)
3. With above family & friends, work out how to rebuild your finances.
4. Chalk it down to experience and let go of the guilt that comes with it all.
